data.title: Analysis-Trump's diesel price relief efforts grow costlier as election nears
data.description:
Oct 23 (Reuters) - With the November midterm elections fast approaching, President Donald Trump is throwing an array of costly and politically fraught solutions at one stubborn problem: the price of diesel.

His administration has offered billions of dollars to farmers, relaxed rules for truckers, eased sanctions on Russian fuel and pressured European allies to release emergency stocks. Yet diesel prices rose again last week, leaving Trump spending political and financial capital without delivering the relief his party wants as voters go to the polls.

Republicans are defending narrow majorities in Congress, and high costs are a major concern for voters. Nearly 80% of Americans blame Trump for higher costs, according to an October Reuters/Ipsos poll. 

US diesel prices rose nearly 10 cents a gallon in the latest week to an average of $6.28, reversing two weeks of declines and remaining near record highs, according to the Energy Information Administration.

Diesel in the last two months has become a central issue not only in the midterms but as a catalyst driving up already-elevated US inflation. The fuel is critical for farmers, construction companies, freight operators and more, and government data last week showed its rise was partly behind hefty increases in delivery costs, early-stage food production costs and even toy prices.

The political pressure is particularly acute in traditionally Republican Farm Belt states like Iowa and Kansas, where rising fuel and fertilizer costs, trade disruptions and weak farm economics have fueled discontent among some of Trump's core supporters.

Trump has promoted his diesel measures at campaign rallies across the region. He signed an executive order onstage in Nebraska allowing red-dyed diesel to be used in highway vehicles and announced $8 billion in new farm aid during a rally in Kansas on Monday.

The measures illustrate the trade-offs Trump is accepting in pursuit of near-term relief. The new aid adds fresh strain on federal spending, while the Russian fuel move risks helping Moscow finance its war in Ukraine. Pressure on European allies to release emergency stocks, backed by a threat to restrict US diesel exports, has created diplomatic friction.

"The president tends to discount long-term losses over short-term gain, and I am skeptical if there is any short gain to be had here," said Chris Borick, a pollster and political scientist at Muhlenberg College in Pennsylvania.

The White House attributed high diesel prices to "pre-existing issues," including years of refinery closures and damage from Russia's war in Ukraine, while defending Trump's efforts to ease costs.

"The President wants diesel prices to fall, which is why he has taken historic actions to save American farmers, truckers, and workers every hard-earned penny," White House spokeswoman Taylor Rogers said.

SKEPTICISM AND UNANSWERED QUESTIONS

One of Trump's most direct attempts to lower diesel costs has struggled to gain traction.

Trump signed an executive order this month allowing truckers to use red-dyed diesel, typically intended for off-road use such as farm equipment, for highway driving while temporarily avoiding certain federal tax reporting and record-keeping requirements.

But the IRS has not eliminated the federal diesel tax, instead temporarily waiving related reporting requirements and penalties through year-end, leaving uncertainty for truck stops and fuel sellers.

David Fialkov, top lobbyist at NATSO, a trade group representing the largest US truck stop operators, said members appreciate Trump's effort to tackle diesel costs but that the guidance remains "murky" and carries too much risk. 

"I really don't see any of these dyed diesel announcements making a meaningful dent in diesel prices," Fialkov said.

Trump is also turning to federal payments to cushion some of the constituencies feeling the pain.

Government payments to farmers were already expected to top $47 billion this year, buoyed by commodity payments and $12 billion in tariff relief distributed by the US Department of Agriculture earlier this year. The $8 billion farm relief program would push the total to a record $55.4 billion, exceeding the previous high of $45 billion in 2020, when farmers received pandemic assistance.

The payments can help farmers manage higher costs and lost sales but do not directly address the market disruptions driving up fuel and fertilizer prices. They also raise questions about taxpayer spending to compensate producers for damage that farm groups say is linked partly to the administration's own trade and foreign policies. 

"This is the second round of emergency aid this year to address losses that were largely foreseeable," National Farmers Union President Rob Larew said. "Trade disruptions and rising fuel costs tied to conflict abroad have put family farmers in a difficult position, and one-time payments can't provide the stability they need to plan for the future."

The aid will arrive after the November 3 election, and likely not reach farmers until the end of the year, USDA official Richard Fordyce told Reuters on Friday. 

FRICTION OVER RUSSIAN FUEL

Some of Trump's efforts to increase diesel supplies carry geopolitical trade-offs.

His decision to ease sanctions on Russian diesel that were designed to restrict Moscow's energy revenues and limit its ability to finance its war in Ukraine has drawn bipartisan criticism -- and raised questions about whether the move will meaningfully lower US fuel prices.

Trump has defended the sanctions relief as necessary to draw Russian President Vladimir Putin into negotiations to end the war in Ukraine and to release American prisoner Stephen Hubbard.

As the administration's intervention efforts have failed to lower fuel costs, Trump has sought to shift blame toward Ukraine and President Volodymyr Zelenskiy rather than the Iran war ahead of the elections.

Analysts say the Iran conflict has been the much bigger driver of the diesel price spike, disrupting global oil flows and refined-fuel supplies, while Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries have helped tighten supplies but played a more limited role in the price.

"I sort of see it as a blame-shifting kind of scapegoating operation, more than a genuine attempt to moderate prices in the lead-up to the election," said Edward Fishman, director of the Maurice R. Greenberg Center at the Council on Foreign Relations.

(Reporting by Jarrett Renshaw and Leah Douglas; Editing by Colleen Jenkins and Deepa Babington)

data.title: Update: US Equity Indexes Fall, Treasury Yields Jump as Iran Tensions Send Crude Oil Sharply Higher
data.description:
04:29 PM EDT, 10/23/2026 (MT Newswires) -- (Updates with index/price moves, macroeconomic data, and geopolitical news from the first paragraph.)

US equity indexes fell, while government yields rose as escalating geopolitical tensions and surging crude oil prices validated concerns in a University of Michigan consumer sentiment survey that inflation will get hotter.

The Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 1.2% to 52,215.16, and the S&P 500 fell 0.5% to 7,623.68. The Nasdaq Composite declined 0.2% to 25,955.34, after trading slightly higher earlier in the session.

Consumer staples, consumer discretionary, and financials led decliners. Energy, technology, and real estate were the only gainers.

Fifteen of the 20 top-performing stocks in a category with market capitalizations exceeding $200 billion each were technology firms, according to data compiled by Finviz. This tech outperformance represents a recovery, as Meta Platforms' ( META ) plans announced Thursday to increase capital expenditure by $5 billion at the bottom end of the range for 2026 and launch a new, non-voting share class to raise funds helped spark a sell-off in the so-called AI trade.

Iran has drawn up detailed plans to target undersea communications cables in the Persian Gulf if the United States and Israel attack it again, two senior Iranian security officials told Reuters. At a campaign rally in Florida, President Donald Trump said he may launch another military campaign against Iran while urging Tehran to agree to US demands to end the war, Al Jazeera, a Middle Eastern broadcaster, reported.

Saudi Aramco, an oil and gas exporter from the Kingdom, has ordered the evacuation of its headquarters in Dhahran on the Gulf near Bahrain as fighting intensified with the Iran-aligned Houthis, Reuters reported.

"Iranian attacks on ships in the Strait of Hormuz, Houthi attacks on the Saudis, Iran's threats to escalate the means of retaliation, and [President Donald] Trump's post about a week ago to 'finish the job' are all contributing to this sentiment," Derek Holt, head of capital market economics at Scotiabank, said in a note.

An oil spill from a tanker was detected off the coast of Umm Al Quwain in the United Arab Emirates, the UAE Ministry of Climate Change and Environment said, without identifying the cause of the spill or the tanker involved, according to a separate Reuters news report.

The front-month West Texas Intermediate crude oil contract jumped 4.3% to $103.70 per barrel, and global benchmark Brent advanced 3.5% to $117.15 per barrel.

The rise in crude prices is adding to inflation concerns and reinforcing expectations that interest rates could remain elevated for longer, a DA Davidson research note said.

US Treasury yields jumped on Friday. The 10-year yield climbed 4.6 basis points to 5%, the 30-year rate advanced 3.9 basis points to 5.33%, and the two-year yield rose 4.9 basis points to 4.68%.

S&P Global's October flash reading of manufacturing conditions rose to 56.0 from 55.9 in September, versus the 55.5 forecast in a Bloomberg-compiled survey, indicating an expansion to a 53-month high.

The final reading in the University of Michigan consumer sentiment index for October stood at 48.0 from the 46.3 preliminary estimate, beating expectations for no revision in a Bloomberg-compiled poll. That print was below the 48.1 final reported in September. Respondents expected a 4.7% inflation rate over the next year and 3.5% annual inflation over the next five years, both up from 4.6% and 3.4%, respectively, in September.

Gold futures fell 1.2% to $4,014.2, and silver futures dropped 1.8% to $54.03.

data.title: TSX Closer: The Index Drops More Than 180 Points as Telecom And Financial Stocks Drag
data.description:
04:29 PM EDT, 10/23/2026 (MT Newswires) -- The S&P/TSX Composite Index fell on Friday as losses in telecom, financial and healthcare stocks outweighed gains in energy, while investors assessed fresh domestic economic data and corporate earnings.

The index closed down 185.27 points, or 0.5%, at 35,788.18, with most sectors down. Telecom led the decliners, dropping 1.4%, followed by financial and healthcare, which dropped 0.9% and 0.8%, respectively. Shares in energy advanced 2.1%, the only sector on the index to move higher.

The Battery Metals Index, which includes companies listed both on the TSX and TSX Venture Exchange, slumped 7.7%.

In commodities, West Texas Intermediate (WTI) and Brent crude prices surged as escalating tensions in the Middle East heightened fears of further oil supply disruptions. Intensifying attacks by Houthi rebels in Saudi Arabia, including threats to energy infrastructure, added to concerns over regional production and exports.

December WTI crude oil contract settled up $3.80, or 3.8%, at $103.27 per barrel, while December Brent oil was last seen up $4.01, or 3.5%, at $117.18 per barrel.

In precious metals, December Comex gold futures dropped 1.1%, or $46.40, to $4,014.00 per ounce at last look.

The US dollar edged down 0.04% against the Canadian dollar to CA$1.4005 at last look.

In economics news, Canadian retail sales climbed 1.2% on the month to CA$74.6 billion in August, with all nine sub-sectors posting gains, according to the country's statistical agency. August's increase was roughly in line with a 1.3% monthly consensus rise from a Bloomberg survey.

Motor vehicle and parts dealers posted the largest sub-sector gain in August, with sales up 1.2% on the month, wrote StatsCan in a statement. New car dealers led the recovery, recording a 1.5% increase after falling 1.4% in July, StatsCan said in a statement.

The statistics agency's preliminary estimate suggests that sales increased 0.7% in September.

Meanwhile, Canadian manufacturing sales edged up 0.1% on the month in September, according to an advance estimate from the Ottawa-based agency.

In stocks, Rogers Communications (RCI-A.TO, RCI-B.TO, RCI) closed down CA$1.07 at CA$45.36 after reporting third-quarter adjusted earnings of CA$1.29 per share earlier Friday, down from CA$1.37 per share a year earlier.

Total revenue for the quarter ended Sept. 30 was CA$5.4 billion compared with CA$5.3 billion a year earlier.

In other corporate news, Bombardier (BBD-A.TO, BBD-B.TO) Friday said it will invest $270 million as part of its US expansion. The funds were earmarked for infrastructure growth, which would result in the hiring of 800 people in Kansas, Texas, Indiana and Connecticut, the jet maker said.

data.title: ENERGY SERVICES OF AMERICA COMPLETES FAMCO ACQUISITION
data.description:
HUNTINGTON, W.Va., Oct. 23, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Energy Services of America Corporation ( ESOA ) (the "Company" or "Energy Services") today announced that its subsidiary, FAMCO Acquisition, Inc., has completed the acquisition of substantially all of the operating assets of FAMCO, Inc. ("FAMCO"), a West Virginia utility contractor focused primarily on water and sewer infrastructure.

The acquisition was completed for a base purchase price of $6.95 million, subject to the adjustments and other terms set forth in the Asset Purchase Agreement. The consideration consists of cash and Energy Services common stock, with a portion of the purchase price withheld pending a post-closing true-up.

FAMCO brings an experienced workforce, equipment fleet and customer relationships in water and sewer infrastructure. The acquisition complements Energy Services' existing water and utility construction operations and expands its capabilities in these markets.

"We are excited to add FAMCO to the Energy Services team," said Douglas Reynolds, President of Energy Services. "FAMCO brings experienced people, equipment and customer relationships that complement our existing operations and further strengthen our capabilities in water and utility construction."

About Energy Services

Energy Services of America Corporation ( ESOA ) , headquartered in Huntington, WV, is a contractor and service company that operates primarily in the mid-Atlantic and Central regions of the United States and provides services to customers in the natural gas, petroleum, water distribution, automotive, chemical, and power industries. Energy Services employs 1,400+ employees on a regular basis. The Company's core values are safety, quality, and production.

data.description:
NEW YORK, Oct 23 (Reuters) - Big AI stocks were mixed on Friday, a day after the biggest decline in the Nasdaq Composite Index in four months, giving investors a welcome respite as they look forward to more information on Anthropic's forthcoming IPO and a further wave of earnings over the next week.

Meta Platforms ( META ), the center of Thursday's storm, was fractionally lower following Thursday's 7% decline. The operator of social media networks and major AI investor said in its earnings report this week that it would create a new class of shares in part to raise money for further capital spending, which was taken as evidence that the next leg of the AI buildout will be costly for shareholders.

Other major AI players were mixed on Friday, with SpaceX, Oracle and Dell Technologies up 1% to 2% and Nvidia, Alphabet and Amazon ( AMZN ) down less than 1%. Big semiconductor stocks were mostly higher after their largest decline since the summer on Thursday.

Credit default swaps tracking the perceived risk of default at the biggest AI players were mostly modestly lower, with Meta's five-year CDS spread trading 0.3% narrower at 123, according to LSEG data. The swaps enable investors to bet on a default using contracts typically with terms of five or 10 years, though contracts frequently change hands for the purposes of hedging positions and betting on near-term market moves.

Thursday's deluge and the day-after calm is the latest sign of indirection in a market that has hovered near record highs without breaking out, said Rick Meckler, partner at Cherry Lane Investments, a family investment office in New Vernon, New Jersey.

"To some extent, we're seeing the market tread water over a longer period of time because every sell-off has been met by buyers and every point upward has been met by sellers," Meckler said.

The Nasdaq was barely changed on Friday afternoon.

Credit-default swap premiums, reflecting the annual cost borne by the swap purchaser in thousands of dollars, have risen over the past year with concern about the risks being taken on by large AI spenders. The premiums rose on Thursday after Meta's decision to sell more stock, as much of the buildout to date has been financed through debt issuance.

The concerns around AI spending and investment returns have added to the market's volatility since Treasury yields rose sharply in August, which changed the economics of investing and bond issuance, given the increasing attractiveness of a higher risk-free rate.

It's been "a very volatile week," said Art Hogan, chief market strategist at B Riley Wealth in Boston. "There's no doubt at some point in time that the higher inflation moves, especially if driven by unsustainably higher energy prices ... would have to show up in corporate earnings. It hasn't yet, but that's the concern. And market participants are trying to position for that."

Shares of neoclouds, smaller companies tied to AI data centers and other infrastructure projects like CoreWeave ( CRWV ), have dropped due to anxiety over their future. Their performance of late has also raised talk on Wall Street that capital is growing scarce - which stands to raise costs further and potentially raise funding issues down the road.

Even so, many investors remain positive on the sector, where giant AI lab Anthropic is expected to publish its IPO prospectus in coming days and Alphabet, Amazon ( AMZN ) and Microsoft ( MSFT ) are expected to report earnings next week.

"In general, AI news in terms of revenues continues to be very strong, it's just at what cost and how long that growth is sustainable," Meckler said. "We really haven't gotten to the point of the market sort of focusing on winners and losers. It's been one big sector trade every day."

(Reporting by Caroline Valetkevitch, editing by Colin Barr, David Gaffen)

data.title: Apple's foldable iPhone hits stores with $2,000 price tag and scarce supply
data.description:
By Aditya Soni, Christine Chen and Will Russell

SYDNEY/SHANGHAI/LONDON, Oct 23 (Reuters) - Apple's ( AAPL ) first folding phone, the iPhone Duo, hit stores around the world on Friday with a price tag of about $2,000 and less of the fanfare that accompanied previous iPhone launches.

From Singapore and Shanghai to London and San Francisco, demand was strong but with sales rationed, there were fewer of the round-the-block queues and overnight camp-outs that once marked new iPhone days.

Competitors such as Samsung Electronics ( SSNLF ) and Huawei Technologies have sold premium foldable phones for years and the Duo is a test of whether Apple ( AAPL ) can reinvent the small foldable mobile market the way the iPhone did for smartphones.

It is also an early challenge for Apple's ( AAPL ) new CEO John Ternus, the former hardware chief who unveiled the phone barely a week after taking charge in September.

Apple's ( AAPL ) estimated delivery dates for the Duo had slipped to late January within minutes of pre-orders opening a week ago, as demand outpaced supply. The US company called the response "nothing short of extraordinary".

Apple ( AAPL ) capped pre-orders at two handsets per customer and limited sales to walk-in shoppers. In China, France, Hong Kong, India and Japan they were only available to those who had ordered online.

In Sydney, where the first Apple ( AAPL ) store began selling the new passport-shaped phones on Friday, a queue formed outside before opening at 8 a.m. local time (2100 GMT).

"This is a bit of a luxury item for me, because it's so expensive, but I just think, you know what? Life's too short," said Simon Krishnan, a 48-year-old engineer who paid A$3,899 ($2,734) for a 512GB Duo.

CEO Ternus played greeter at a store in Austin, Texas, throwing open the doors and high-fiving customers as they streamed in, a video posted on X by CBS Austin showed.

A known car enthusiast, Ternus's Austin visit coincides with this weekend's Formula 1 US Grand Prix in the city, with Apple ( AAPL ) holding exclusive US broadcast and streaming rights to the racing series.

At Apple's ( AAPL ) Fifth Avenue store in New York, marketing head Greg Joswiak opened the doors to a crowd of customers, social media posts showed. Some posts said people had camped outside the store since as early as 4 a.m. local time (0800 GMT).

Mohit Chandel, a 32-year-old San Francisco resident and consultant, had promised his father in Singapore an iPhone Duo for his retirement but forgot to pre-order one.

So when he spotted a dozen people lining up outside an Apple ( AAPL ) store around 11 p.m. Thursday, he joined them, ordered a bench and pillow from Walgreens and settled in for the night.

"He doesn't know that. All the pre-orders are gone. He's expecting a Duo sometime in the mail so now I have to buy it," Chandel said.

In China, a soft consumer market and rising memory costs have led to six straight quarters of declining smartphone shipments, although Apple's ( AAPL ) market share has rebounded as some buyers trade up to premium devices.

Liu Wei, a 26-year-old healthcare professional, already has a foldable phone from Xiaomi, but still queued outside a Shanghai store from 6 a.m. for Apple's ( AAPL ) first foldable.

"I've used Apple ( AAPL ) products for many years and I have more trust (in the brand), so I bought one on launch day to try it out," he said.

Many queued to pick up pre-orders, while others hoped for limited stock or to browse display models.

Others were resellers.

In Hong Kong, May, 38, who declined to give his full name, bought a 256GB iPhone Duo, priced at HK$17,499 ($2,231.73), in an online pre-sale and planned to resell it for a profit of around HK$4,000. "A few meals' worth of money," he joked.

Paul Francis, 53, was one of several dozen fans who queued overnight outside London's Regent Street store in pouring rain.

"Some people think it was mad. Including myself," the charity manager said.

MIXED REVIEWS

Early reviews have praised the Duo's design as well as its sturdy and barely visible hinge, a major feat for phones whose prominent creased screen has long been a drawback and potential deterrent for buyers.

But reviewers said camera compromises, including no telephoto lens, and third-party apps still to be reworked for the new display size could disappoint some buyers.

They also said the folded Duo is less handy for the quick tasks most users do daily and several prominent reviewers recommended against it for many Apple ( AAPL ) customers.

"It's been a lot of fun trying the Duo out for a week, but it feels like I've gotten to use an extraordinarily polished prototype - not a finished product that I'd want to buy and carry," wrote longtime Apple ( AAPL ) commentator John Gruber.

Tech commentator Marques Brownlee said in a YouTube review that for a regular person who mostly texts and browses, "it is probably a no. But if the $2,000 doesn't mean much to you, and you like the idea, after the learning curve and getting used to not having facial identification, it is a really fun phone."

In Berlin, YouTube content creator Patrick Wolter was impressed that the Duo works as a phone and an iPad in one.

"I've always found it a hassle to carry around a separate tablet, especially since I already have a laptop and other gear," he said. "In the long run, this will likely end up replacing those other devices."

TOUGH TO FIND

Apple's ( AAPL ) entry into the relatively niche foldables market could bring the format to a much broader audience, said Francisco Jeronimo, vice president at market researcher IDC.

IDC expects Apple ( AAPL ) will take 44% of the foldable market value in 2026 on 31% of units. By 2027, it will become the market leader both in value and units shipped, IDC forecast.

"Apple ( AAPL ) has made a convincing case for this form factor," Jeronimo said after spending a week with the Duo.

"Now comes the next test: turning excitement into availability, adoption and a lasting new chapter for the smartphone market," Jeronimo said.

($1 = 1.4257 Australian dollars)

($1 = 7.8410 Hong Kong dollars)

(Reporting by Aditya Soni in Bengaluru, Stephen Nellis and Nathan Frandino in San Francisco, Nicoco Chan in Shanghai, Joyce Zhou in Hong Kong, Christine Chen in Sydney, Matthias Baehr in Berlin, Will Russell and Ben Makori in London, additional reporting by Anhata Rooprai in Bengaluru; Editing by Will Dunham, Christopher Cushing, Kate Mayberry, Alexander Smith and Leroy Leo)

data.title: CVS is trying out pharmacists in chronic health management
data.description:
NASHVILLE, Oct 23 (Reuters) - CVS Health ( CVS ) Chief Medical Officer Dr. Amy Compton-Phillips on Friday said healthcare affordability and access could potentially improve if pharmacists in its 9,000 retail stores play a bigger role in chronic disease management, helping consumers stay on top of their most important health metrics.

Each year, millions of Americans die from heart attacks, strokes, kidney disease, diabetes and other chronic conditions that can be treated with medical attention and proper medicines, she said.

"We want to make it really easy and convenient for you to know your numbers," she said, adding that the company is experimenting with how pharmacists could become more involved by taking measurements for blood pressure, cholesterol, and blood sugar.

CVS is starting now with a pilot in five stores in Michigan to try out the concept, she said. In the US, the role of pharmacists is determined in part by varying state pharmacy regulations.

CVS Health ( CVS ) is one of the largest US healthcare conglomerates, with the Aetna health insurance company, CVS Caremark pharmacy benefit manager and a nationwide network of retail pharmacies under its corporate umbrella.

Compton-Phillips, speaking during the Reuters Total Health conference in Nashville, said the company was also talking to the government's Medicare agency about the role pharmacists could play in expanding access to healthcare and providing lower-cost healthcare.

Affordability of healthcare is a key issue for the Trump administration, which is experimenting with different pilots that could lower costs for the more than 70 million people enrolled in the Medicare program for people aged 65 and older or with disabilities.

One of the pilots involves more access to highly popular GLP-1 medications used to treat obesity, which the government has made available for $50 a month for a limited time through TrumpRx.gov.

More companies, however, are cutting corporate coverage of the medicines in 2027, recent surveys show, concerned about the increased cost to their health plans for the Eli Lilly ( LLY ) and Novo Nordisk medicines such as Mounjaro, Zepbound, Ozempic and Wegovy.

Those medicines cost a few hundred dollars on the drugmakers' direct-pay websites, but can be more expensive to employers when they are covered in their insurance plans.

Compton-Phillips said she would like to see better access to the GLP-1 drugs at a lower cost, describing their potential health benefits as "incredible."

"They really do have real benefits in decreasing heart disease and kidney disease," she said.

"I can't wait until 2032," she said. "That's when Ozempic goes generic in the US and I think we are going to be writing prescriptions for it like water."

data.title: Exclusive-First Russian diesel from Putin-Trump deal heading for US, data shows
data.description:
Oct 23 (Reuters) - The first Russian diesel bound for the US following a surprise agreement reached between Moscow and US President Donald Trump is aboard a tanker heading for New York, ship-tracking data showed on Friday.

Trump announced the deal this month as part of his efforts to bring down soaring diesel prices ahead of November 3 US midterm elections.

Trump also waived parts of a new US sanctions law against Russia and threatened Europe with a US diesel export ban unless countries released more from their emergency reserves to help ease prices.

The Malta-flagged medium-sized tanker Agioi Fanendes was loaded with 40,000 metric tons of ultra-low sulphur diesel in Russia's Baltic port of Primorsk on October 22, according to LSEG shipping data. It is expected to arrive in the United States on November 7.

The identity of the buyer and seller were not immediately known. The cargo will be the first imported by the US since former President Joe Biden announced a ban on US imports of Russian oil and petroleum products in 2022.

Trump announced on October 9 that Russia would immediately export 300,000 metric tons, or 2.25 million barrels, to the US and global markets, followed by 500,000 tons in November and 1 million tons "immediately thereafter".

A Kremlin spokesperson on Friday confirmed a first ship under the deal had departed, but did not specify whether it was bound for the US market or elsewhere.

"As far as I'm aware, there have already been reports from the Ministry of Energy that the first tanker has, in fact, set sail for its recipients, its buyers. Further shipments will continue at a steady pace from here on," Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said on a daily conference call.

The deal with the US involved Russia lifting a self-imposed ban on diesel exports.

RUSSIA RESUMING GLOBAL EXPORTSSince the EU imposed a full embargo on imports of Russian oil products in February 2023 over the war in Ukraine, Russia has exported diesel mainly to Turkey and Brazil, as well as to African countries.

It also supplies Central Asia by rail.

Shipping data from LSEG and Kpler published this week showed Russian diesel cargoes resuming voyages to their traditional destinations after Moscow lifted its own ban, with at least two tankers signalling trips to Turkey and Brazil.

It was unclear where other tankers were destined for, with cargoes loaded in Primorsk signalling Gibraltar, the Atlantic Coast or Port Said, LSEG data showed.

Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak has said additional US shipments would follow as companies from the two countries work out the necessary contracts.

Putin envoy Kirill Dmitriev, who also heads Russia's sovereign wealth fund, said last week that the US Treasury had asked the fund to help sort out tricky payment issues relating to the agreement.

That account was not accurate, a source familiar with the matter said.

Novak has said that Russia would be able to increase its diesel exports to its usual levels of 3-3.5 million tons per month by year-end.

(Reporting by Reuters; editing by Philippa Fletcher and Jason Neely)

data.title: Democrat on US FCC urges broadcast industry to be more aggressive confronting the agency
data.description:
WASHINGTON, Oct 23 (Reuters) - The sole Democratic member of the Federal Communications Commission on Friday urged the broadcast industry to take a more aggressive approach in confronting the Trump administration's actions toward major US networks and stations.

FCC Commissioner Anna Gomez called on the National Association of Broadcasters to address the administration's efforts to challenge broadcasters on a series of fronts, including a warning from FCC Chair Brendan Carr that US broadcast networks could violate their regulatory obligations by airing "entirely fake polls" before the November 3 election.

"This administration is running a coordinated, government-wide effort to reshape the media into its sanctioned messenger," Gomez warned, adding that Carr was seeking to pressure networks into not running polls the administration dislikes, which she said was not proper.

Carr, who has repeatedly faced pressure from President Donald Trump to crack down on ⁠US broadcasters and journalists, in April ordered an unprecedented early license review for all eight of Disney's ( DIS ) company-owned ABC TV stations.

A spokesperson for Carr did not immediately comment.

NAB President Curtis LeGeyt said in a statement that the group appreciated Gomez's "recognition of the value of local broadcasters and her commitment to the First Amendment principles that underpin a free press."

"We will continue working with her and all policymakers to protect broadcasters' rights," he said.

Gomez said the NAB had been "largely quiet through the first year of this censorship and control campaign" but that it had not stayed "completely silent."

An "industry confronting a coordinated effort to turn licensing authority into leverage over election-year coverage needs more than a couple of tempered statements," she added.

In April, the NAB said the Disney ( DIS ) early-renewal decision "creates ‌significant uncertainty for all broadcasters" and argued the "FCC must be careful to avoid actions that create further instability for the local stations viewers and listeners depend on."

The FCC also said earlier this ⁠year that ​late-night and daytime talk shows are no longer bona fide news programs ​that are exempt from equal-time rules for interviews with political candidates.

data.title: Chili's workers' lawsuit looks to strike New York state's lower wage for tipped workers
data.description:
Oct 23 (Reuters) - A lawsuit filed on Friday involving the pay practices of Chili's ( EAT ) operator Brinker International ( EAT ) is seeking to strike down New York state's lower minimum wage for workers who earn tips, which it claims fuels the sexual and racial harassment of workers.

The proposed class action in federal court in Brooklyn by three former Chili's employees claims that New York's policy, which most other US states share, allows Brinker ( EAT ) to force employees to rely on tips and exposes them to unlawful discrimination.

"Brinker ( EAT ) promotes a culture in which tipped service employees make customers 'feel special,' even at the expense of their dignity and safety," the lawsuit says.

Brinker ( EAT ) did not respond to a request for comment. The New York Attorney General's office did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the challenge to the state law. 

Many worker advocates have for years called for the elimination of sub-minimum wages that companies may pay to workers who earn tips under federal and most state laws, as long as tips make up the difference. 

In New York, where the minimum wage is $16 an hour or $17 in and around New York City, food service workers who earn tips may be paid $10.70 or $11.35 an hour. The federal tipped minimum wage is $2.13 an hour, compared with the traditional minimum wage of $7.25, and applies in states that do not set their own minimums.

RELYING ON TIPS

Advocates say that because tips are discretionary and unpredictable, they should supplement workers' incomes rather than make up most of their pay. The lawsuit against Brinker ( EAT ) says that relying on tips forces workers to tolerate conduct such as sexual harassment and customers' potential racial bias.

The plaintiffs' lawyers said in the lawsuit that they plan to expand the case to include a nationwide class of Chili's ( EAT ) workers.

Brinker ( EAT ) operates more than 1,200 Chili's ( EAT ) restaurants in the US, including 36 in New York. The company also owns Maggiano's Little Italy ( EAT ), an Italian restaurant chain with about 50 US locations.

The lawsuit claims that Chili's ( EAT ) reliance on customer ratings to determine workers' schedules, shifts and table assignments is also unlawful. The ratings system can be racially biased, the lawsuit says, and can make it difficult for servers to reject unwanted advances from customers for fear of a poor rating.

The named plaintiffs, three former employees at a Chili's ( EAT ) in the Glendale section of Queens in New York City, claim they were routinely subjected to sexual advances and inappropriate comments and that management did not adequately protect workers from harassment.

(Reporting by Daniel Wiessner in Albany, New York, Editing by Alexia Garamfalvi and Rod Nickel)

data.title: US to remove 50% tariffs on some Canadian goods to help Republicans in midterms, WSJ reports
data.description:
Oct 23 (Reuters) - The United States is expected to remove 50% tariffs on some Canadian agricultural and forestry products in a bid to help Maine Senator Susan Collins and other Republicans from northern US states in the upcoming midterm elections, the Wall Street Journal reported on Friday, citing people familiar.

The reductions could be balanced out by raising levies on other Canadian goods, the report said, adding that a proclamation altering the tariffs could come as early as Friday.

A White House official told the Journal that any tariff announcements would come directly from the administration and that any preliminary reporting is speculation. The White House didn't immediately respond to a Reuters request for comment.

Senator Collins, in a statement issued shortly after the WSJ report, said that nine categories of products, including blueberry, potato, apple, and seaweed producers, will be exempted from U.S. tariffs on Canada.

The Commerce Department did not immediately provide a comment on her announcement, which comes as she is trying to win a sixth term to the senate in Democratic-leaning Maine.

Republican candidates in ​northern US border states most affected by the tariffs are trying to strike a balance between appealing to Trump's loyal base and winning independent voters.

The economies of Michigan and Maine have long been intertwined with Canada's, covering everything from auto parts to lumber to fruit-picking equipment. That has raised the stakes in two states that Republicans will likely need to win in the November 3 elections if they are to hold the US Senate.

US President Donald Trump ​said on Friday that Canada is ‌working on a trade deal with the United States, though the two nations ​have been locked in a ​standoff since talks broke down in August, triggering new ‌tariffs ⁠and retaliation on both sides of the border.

(Reporting by Kanjyik Ghosh in Barcelona;)

data.description:
02:03 PM EDT, 10/23/2026 (MT Newswires) -- (Updates with index/price moves, macroeconomic data, and company/geopolitical news from the first paragraph.)

US equity indexes traded mixed as escalating geopolitical tensions and rising energy prices weighed on risk appetite, partially offsetting small gains in technology.

The Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 1.2% to 52,255.1, and the S&P 500 declined 0.4% to 7,631.2 after midday Friday. The Nasdaq Composite was less than 0.1% higher at 25,988.3.

All but two sectors declined, led by consumer staples. Energy and technology were the only sectors to rise.

Fifteen of the 20 top-performing stocks in a category with a market capitalization exceeding $200 billion each were from technology, according to data compiled by Finviz. This tech outperformance represents a recovery, as Meta Platforms' (META) plans announced Thursday to increase capital expenditure by $5 billion at the bottom end of the range for 2026 and launch a new, non-voting share class to raise funds helped spark a sell-off in the so-called AI trade.

"Investors continued to assess the recent selloff in AI-related stocks, driven by concerns over the sector's substantial capital requirements," D.A. Davidson said in a research note. "Although the pace of the decline in technology stocks moderated, escalating geopolitical tensions and rising energy prices kept risk appetite subdued."

Saudi Aramco has ordered the evacuation of its headquarters in Dhahran on the Gulf near Bahrain, Reuters reported, as fighting intensified with the Iran-aligned Houthis, Reuters reported. Meanwhile, an oil spill from a tanker was detected off the coast of Umm Al Quwain in the United Arab Emirates, the UAE Ministry of Climate Change and Environment said, according to the news report, without identifying the cause of the spill or the tanker involved.

The front-month West Texas Intermediate crude oil contract jumped 3.8% to $103.29 per barrel, and global benchmark Brent advanced 3.1% to $116.62 per barrel.

"Iranian attacks on ships in the Strait of Hormuz, Houthi attacks on the Saudis, Iran's threats to escalate the means of retaliation, and [President Donald] Trump's post about a week ago to 'finish the job' are all contributing to this sentiment," Derek Holt, head of capital market economics at Scotiabank, said in a note.

The rise in crude prices is adding to inflation concerns and reinforcing expectations that interest rates could remain elevated for longer, the D.A. Davidson note said.

US Treasury yields jumped in midday trading. The 10-year yield climbed 3.1 basis points to 4.98%, the 30-year rate advanced 2.4 basis points to 5.31%, and the two-year yield rose 5.1 basis points to 4.67%.

S&P Global's October flash reading of manufacturing conditions rose to 56.0 from 55.9 in September, versus the 55.5 forecast in a Bloomberg-compiled survey, indicating an expansion to a 53-month high.

The final reading in the University of Michigan consumer sentiment index for October stood at 48.0 from the 46.3 preliminary estimate, beating expectations for no revision in a Bloomberg-compiled poll. That print was below the 48.1 final reported in September. Respondents expected a 4.7% inflation rate over the next year and 3.5% annual inflation over the next five years, both up from 4.6% and 3.4%, respectively, in September.

Gold futures fell 1.3% to $4,008.20, and silver futures dropped 1.8% to $54.02.
